newsitem.title: UK: Sour oil heads east despite Iraq absence in the Med.
newsitem.headline: Sour oil heads east despite Iraq absence in the Med.

text.p: Producers of sour crude oil are not rushing to sell into a strong Mediterranean crude market because Asia still offers better value and the immediate future of Iraqi exports remains unclear, traders said on Thursday.
Producers like Saudi Arabia and Iran might have been expected to take advantage of the vacuum created by looming delays to fresh Iraqi exports by diverting incremental barrels from Asia, they said.
But a narrow differential between regional benchmarks Brent and Dubai means profits in Asia are stronger than in the Mediterranean and it pays to keep barrels going East, traders said.

"Premiums are strengthening in the Med but the outright value is better in Asia. Unless something changes there is no reason to have any extra crude here if they can have $1 to $2 a barrel more in Asia," he said.
Asian crude buyers have come back into the market with a vengeance after a period of unusually extensive refinery maintenance in the region.
"The problem is availability -- the Far East is so attractive that barrels automatically move there," said an official at a sour producer that normally competes with Russian Urals.

The result is that, barring a virtual collapse of the U.N. oil for food programme, Russian Urals is likely to remain the dominant sour in the Med, while Iraqi Kirkuk remains off the market, traders said.
A Mediterranean crude trader said: "It would take quite a long time for other sour producers to send barrels to us. And in any case, no one knows how long Iraq is going to stay out."

The collapse of Brent last week halved the August differential between Brent and Dubai from previous weeks to around 60 cents per barrel early this week, although it widened to around 80 cents on Thursday.

The narrowed differential -- down from the average for 1997 so far of $1.40 a barrel and around the lowest for two years -- has prompted Asian refiners to boost demand for crudes priced against Dated Brent.

Asian demand has risen most noticeably for West African grades, which analysts say flowed to Asia at an average daily rate in May of 770,000 barrels per day (bpd) or 30 percent above early 1996 levels.
These flows cut the availability of West African grades in the Atlantic basin and thus tightened Mediterranean supply, providing support for the differentials for all grades supplied to the region.
Mediterranean sours have not matched Asia's blistering pace. Urals has risen to around Dated Brent -95 cents from -$1.15 a week ago on tight supply and solid demand.
More support has come from disputes between Iraq and the United Nations over weapons inspection which have gathered pace and uncertainty has mounted over the future of the oil for food programme.

The oil deal was renewed two weeks ago but oil sales for the second six-month period beginning June 8 cannot begin until the distribution plan and a pricing formula for oil contracts is submitted to the U.N..

Confusion deepened on Wednesday when an Iraqi official said the aid distribution plan was ready for submission but that oil sales under the U.N. "oil-for-food" deal would not begin until the money currently held in an escrow account was spent.
When Iraq does decide to resume sales, traders say its crude is easily available.
"And bear in mind that Ceyhan is stuffed with Kirkuk and the Iraqis can resume loadings very swiftly."
